items.prompt: Define acceleration.
items.canonical_answer: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, a = (v − u) ÷ t, a vector with unit m s⁻².
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the definition names rate of change of velocity with its equation and unit m s⁻². "Rate of change of speed" drops the vector nature and does not carry the mark.
items.provenance: Authored for CIE 9702 AS Physics topic 2 from the topic claim ledger and work order.
objective_titles: define and use distance, displacement, speed, velocity and acceleration

items.prompt: A cyclist rides 750 m east along a straight road in 2.5 × 10² s, then rides 250 m west in 50 s. Calculate the magnitude of her average velocity for the whole journey.
items.canonical_answer: Displacement: 750 − 250 = 500 m east. Total time: 2.5 × 10² + 50 = 300 s. Average velocity = displacement ÷ total time, so 500 ÷ 300 = 1.67 m s⁻¹ east, which is 1.7 m s⁻¹ to two significant figures.
marking_guidance: Equation and working: displacement found as 500 m east and the total time as 300 s, then velocity = displacement ÷ time - 1 mark (the first step).
Final answer: 1.7 m s⁻¹ east with the unit and two significant figures - 1 mark. Dividing the 1000 m distance by 300 s gives 3.3 m s⁻¹, the average speed, not the velocity.
items.provenance: Authored for CIE 9702 AS Physics topic 2 from the topic claim ledger and work order.
objective_titles: define and use distance, displacement, speed, velocity and acceleration

items.prompt: A learner says that because the minibus ended where it began, its average velocity for the trip can be worked out from the distance on the meter. Explain the error.
items.canonical_answer: Distance on the meter is a scalar total, but velocity is defined from displacement, a vector. The journey ended where it began, so the displacement is zero and the average velocity is zero, while the distance travelled is large. The test is whether the direction changed during the motion: because it did, distance cannot stand in for displacement.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the error named - distance, a scalar, wrongly used where displacement, a vector, is required; the displacement here is zero, so the velocity is zero, whereas the meter's distance gives only the average speed.
items.provenance: Authored for CIE 9702 AS Physics topic 2 from the topic claim ledger and work order.
objective_titles: define and use distance, displacement, speed, velocity and acceleration

items.prompt: State one feature of acceleration that shows it is a vector, and one situation in which a body is accelerating although its speed is not changing.
items.canonical_answer: Acceleration has a direction as well as a magnitude, so its sign depends on the direction chosen as positive. A body moving in a circle at a steady speed is accelerating, because its direction of travel is changing, so its velocity is changing even though the speed is not.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: a named vector feature (magnitude together with direction, or the sign depending on the positive direction) and a situation of changing direction at constant speed, such as motion around a bend.
items.provenance: Authored for CIE 9702 AS Physics topic 2 from the topic claim ledger and work order.
objective_titles: define and use distance, displacement, speed, velocity and acceleration

items.prompt: State the difference between the distance travelled by a body and its displacement.
items.canonical_answer: Distance is the total length of the path travelled, a scalar; displacement is the distance moved in a stated direction from the starting point, a vector. They are equal only for a journey that never changes direction.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the distinction - distance is the scalar path length whereas displacement is the vector distance in a stated direction from the start; both carry the contrast that direction counts for one and not the other.
items.provenance: Authored for CIE 9702 AS Physics topic 2 from the topic claim ledger and work order.
objective_titles: define and use distance, displacement, speed, velocity and acceleration

items.prompt: A displacement–time graph is a straight line from the origin to the point (12 s, 84 m). Determine what the graph shows about the motion, with its value.
items.canonical_answer: A straight displacement–time line means constant velocity. The graph shows uniform motion at v = ∆s ÷ ∆t, so 84 ÷ 12 = 7.0 m s⁻¹. The line starting at the origin means the body set out from its starting point at t = 0.
marking_guidance: Reading the graph: the straight line through the origin is identified as constant velocity from its shape and values - 1 mark.
What the gradient means: the value from 84 ÷ 12 is 7.0 m s⁻¹, so the graph shows uniform velocity of 7.0 m s⁻¹ - 1 mark.
items.provenance: Authored for CIE 9702 AS Physics topic 2 from the topic claim ledger and work order.
objective_titles: use graphical methods to represent distance, displacement, speed, velocity and acceleration

items.prompt: A jogger runs 400 m once around a circular track and finishes where she started. Her distance–time graph and her displacement–time graph are drawn for the run. Determine how the two graphs differ over the same interval.
items.canonical_answer: The distance–time graph rises steadily and cannot fall, because distance adds along the whole path; it ends at 400 m. The displacement–time graph rises, then falls back to zero at the finish, because displacement is the vector distance from the starting point, and she ends where she began. The two graphs agree only while she runs the first stretch away from the start.
marking_guidance: Reading the graphs: the distance graph rises throughout and ends at 400 m - 1 mark.

What the difference shows: the displacement graph returns to zero at the finish because the direction of motion changed around the loop, so the graph can fall where the distance graph cannot - 1 mark.
items.provenance: Authored for CIE 9702 AS Physics topic 2 from the topic claim ledger and work order.
objective_titles: use graphical methods to represent distance, displacement, speed, velocity and acceleration

items.prompt: A forklift at a Windhoek warehouse moves with a velocity that rises uniformly from 1.5 m s⁻¹ to 4.5 m s⁻¹ in 6.0 s, and then holds 4.5 m s⁻¹ for a further 4.0 s. From a sketch-graph method, determine the total distance it advances.
items.canonical_answer: Graph: velocity in m s⁻¹ against time in s, a straight line from (0, 1.5) to (6.0, 4.5), then horizontal to (10, 4.5). Phase 1 is a rectangle plus a triangle: the rectangle is 1.5 m s⁻¹ by 6.0 s, which is 9.0 m, and the triangle of height 3.0 m s⁻¹ on the same base adds 9.0 m, giving 18 m. Phase 2 is a rectangle: 4.5 × 4.0 = 18 m. Total: 18 + 18 = 36 m.
marking_guidance: Equation and working: the area split into rectangle and triangle, so 9.0 + 9.0 = 18 m and 4.5 × 4.0 = 18 m - 1 mark for the substitution step shown.
Final answer: 36 m with the unit - 1 mark. Taking phase 1 as one triangle alone gives 9.0 m and drops the rectangle under the starting velocity.
items.provenance: Authored for CIE 9702 AS Physics topic 2 from the topic claim ledger and work order.
objective_titles: use graphical methods to represent distance, displacement, speed, velocity and acceleration

items.prompt: A learner has to sketch, in words, a distance–time graph for a bus that reverses 100 m into a depot. He proposes a line that falls back towards zero during the reverse. Explain why his sketch cannot be right.
items.canonical_answer: This situation cannot produce a falling distance graph, because distance is the total path length and it keeps adding while the bus moves, whichever way it goes. During the reverse the displacement falls, so it is a displacement–time graph that slopes downwards there. The graph he describes belongs to displacement, since a falling line requires a quantity that counts direction.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the reason - distance is a running total of path length, so a fall in the line would mean negative path; in this case only the displacement–time graph falls, because displacement counts direction.
items.provenance: Authored for CIE 9702 AS Physics topic 2 from the topic claim ledger and work order.
objective_titles: use graphical methods to represent distance, displacement, speed, velocity and acceleration

items.prompt: State the features of the line on a velocity–time graph for a body whose acceleration is uniform, and say what each feature shows.
items.canonical_answer: The line is straight and sloping, and the slope is constant: the gradient is the acceleration, one value holding along the whole line. A steeper line shows a larger acceleration. The height of the line shows the velocity, and the area under it shows the displacement.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the features - a straight sloping line, whose constant gradient is the uniform acceleration; the height and the area are named as velocity and displacement.
items.provenance: Authored for CIE 9702 AS Physics topic 2 from the topic claim ledger and work order.
objective_titles: use graphical methods to represent distance, displacement, speed, velocity and acceleration

items.prompt: State the difference between the distance–time graph and the displacement–time graph of the same return journey, such as a walk out to a shop and straight back.
items.canonical_answer: Both rise during the walk out. On the walk back the distance–time graph keeps rising, because distance adds along the path, while the displacement–time graph falls back to zero, because the walker is returning to the starting point. The distance graph ends above zero; the displacement graph ends at zero.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the contrast - the distance graph cannot fall and ends at the full path length, whereas the displacement graph falls back to zero on the return leg because displacement is measured from the start with direction.
items.provenance: Authored for CIE 9702 AS Physics topic 2 from the topic claim ledger and work order.
objective_titles: use graphical methods to represent distance, displacement, speed, velocity and acceleration

items.prompt: A motion graph is set to be described in words for another learner to plot. Explain why the description must give the quantity and unit on each axis, not just the shape of the line.
items.canonical_answer: The axis labels fix what the graph means: a rising straight line is constant velocity on a displacement–time graph but constant acceleration on a velocity–time graph, so the same shape carries different physics. Without the quantity and its unit on each axis the plotter cannot label the axes, scale them, or read any value from the line, and the key values that start and end the line have no units to carry.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the reason - the axes fix the meaning of the shape and the units of every value, because the same line means different things on differently labelled axes, so the purpose of the description is lost without them.
items.provenance: Authored for CIE 9702 AS Physics topic 2 from the topic claim ledger and work order.
objective_titles: use graphical methods to represent distance, displacement, speed, velocity and acceleration

items.prompt: A lift rises from rest. Its velocity–time graph is a straight line from (0, 0) to (5.0 s, 2.0 m s⁻¹), then horizontal to (14 s, 2.0 m s⁻¹). Determine the displacement of the lift in the 14 s.
items.canonical_answer: The displacement is the area between the line and the time axis. The ramp is a triangle of height 2.0 m s⁻¹ and base 5.0 s: its area is 5.0 m. The steady stretch is a rectangle: 2.0 × 9.0 = 18 m. Total: 5.0 + 18 = 23 m upward.
marking_guidance: Reading the graph: the area split into the triangle 5.0 m and the rectangle 18 m - 1 mark.
What the area gives: the displacement, 5.0 + 18 = 23 m upward - 1 mark.
items.provenance: Authored for CIE 9702 AS Physics topic 2 from the topic claim ledger and work order.
objective_titles: determine displacement from the area under a velocity–time graph

items.prompt: A cart's velocity–time graph is a horizontal line at −3.0 m s⁻¹ from t = 0 to t = 8.0 s. Determine its displacement in that interval, and what the sign of your answer means.
items.canonical_answer: The displacement is the area between the line and the time axis: (−3.0) × 8.0 = −24 m. The negative sign means the cart is 24 m back along the positive direction from where it started, because a velocity below the axis is motion in the negative direction, and its area subtracts from the displacement.
marking_guidance: Reading the graph: the area taken as 3.0 × 8.0 below the axis - 1 mark.
What the value means: the displacement is −24 m, the minus showing travel in the negative direction, so the cart ends 24 m on the negative side of its start - 1 mark.
items.provenance: Authored for CIE 9702 AS Physics topic 2 from the topic claim ledger and work order.
objective_titles: determine displacement from the area under a velocity–time graph

items.prompt: A goods train accelerates uniformly from rest for 30 s and reaches 12 m s⁻¹. Using the area under its velocity–time line, determine the distance travelled in that time, and check it with s = ½at².
items.canonical_answer: The line runs from (0, 0) to (30, 12): the area is a triangle, ½ × 12 × 30 = 180 m. Check: a = ∆v ÷ ∆t, so 12 ÷ 30 = 0.40 m s⁻², and s = ½at² with a = 0.40 m s⁻² and t² = 900 s² gives 180 m. Both give 180 m.
marking_guidance: Equation and working: the area as ½ × 12 × 30, then the check with a = 12 ÷ 30 = 0.40 m s⁻² substituted into s = ½at² - 1 mark for the steps shown.
Final answer: 180 m by both routes, with the unit - 1 mark.
items.provenance: Authored for CIE 9702 AS Physics topic 2 from the topic claim ledger and work order.
objective_titles: determine displacement from the area under a velocity–time graph

items.prompt: A drone flies at 2.0 m s⁻¹ for 5.0 s, then rises faster and faster, so the tail of its velocity–time graph curves upward. Explain why its displacement grows more in each later second than in the second before.
items.canonical_answer: The displacement gained in any second is the area under the velocity–time line over that second. In this situation the curve climbs higher as time goes on, so each later strip of area is taller than the one before it, and each second adds a bigger slice. The displacement therefore grows faster than steadily, because the area per second is the velocity, and the velocity itself is increasing.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the reasoning for this case - each second's displacement is its strip of area, which is the velocity times the time, so because the curve rises the strips grow and the displacement grows by more each second.
items.provenance: Authored for CIE 9702 AS Physics topic 2 from the topic claim ledger and work order.
objective_titles: determine displacement from the area under a velocity–time graph

items.prompt: A train pulls out of a station already moving at 4.0 m s⁻¹ and reaches 10 m s⁻¹ after 25 s of uniform acceleration. A learner finds the displacement from a velocity–time sketch as ½ × 10 × 25 = 125 m. Explain the error and give the correct displacement.
items.canonical_answer: The error is taking the area as one triangle: the line does not start from the origin, because the motion starts at 4.0 m s⁻¹, not at rest. The whole area is a rectangle of 4.0 × 25 = 100 m beneath the starting velocity plus a triangle of height 6.0 m s⁻¹ and base 25 s, which is 75 m, on top, so the displacement is 175 m, not 125 m. The test is whether the line starts from the origin; here it does not, so the rectangle under the starting velocity must be counted.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the error named - a triangle taken where the line starts at a non-zero velocity, so the rectangle under u is dropped; in fact the area is 100 + 75 = 175 m, and the test is that the line does not start from the origin.
items.provenance: Authored for CIE 9702 AS Physics topic 2 from the topic claim ledger and work order.
objective_titles: determine displacement from the area under a velocity–time graph

items.prompt: Define what the area under a velocity–time graph represents, and give its unit.
items.canonical_answer: The area between the velocity–time line and the time axis represents the displacement over that interval; its unit is the metre, from m s⁻¹ multiplied by s.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the definition - the area gives the displacement, with the unit m named from the axes multiplied together.
items.provenance: Authored for CIE 9702 AS Physics topic 2 from the topic claim ledger and work order.
objective_titles: determine displacement from the area under a velocity–time graph

items.prompt: State two features of an area under a velocity–time graph that must be checked before the area is read off as a displacement.
items.canonical_answer: Whether the area is split into whole rectangles and triangles whose corners lie on the line, and whether any part of it lies below the time axis, since that part is a negative velocity and subtracts from the displacement.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: two features named - the split into shapes with corners on the line, and the sign of areas below the axis, which count as negative displacement.
items.provenance: Authored for CIE 9702 AS Physics topic 2 from the topic claim ledger and work order.
objective_titles: determine displacement from the area under a velocity–time graph

items.prompt: State the difference between finding displacement from a velocity–time graph that starts from rest and one that starts at a non-zero velocity.
items.canonical_answer: From rest, the whole area is a single triangle to the origin. From a non-zero start, the area is a rectangle beneath the starting velocity together with a shape above it; both must be added. The difference is the rectangle under u: it exists in the second case and not in the first.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the contrast - a triangle to the origin when the line starts at rest, whereas a non-zero start adds the rectangle under u, and both areas are needed for the whole displacement.
items.provenance: Authored for CIE 9702 AS Physics topic 2 from the topic claim ledger and work order.
objective_titles: determine displacement from the area under a velocity–time graph

items.prompt: Explain why the area under a velocity–time graph has the unit of distance, so that it can be read as a displacement at all.
items.canonical_answer: The area is found by multiplying a height in m s⁻¹ by a width in s, and m s⁻¹ multiplied by s leaves metres. That matches the definition of velocity: displacement equals velocity multiplied by time, so the area is that product collected over the interval, strip by strip. The purpose of reading the area is precisely this: it returns the quantity whose rate of change the height shows.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the reason - the unit of the area is m s⁻¹ × s = m because velocity times time is a displacement, so the area is needed as the quantity the definition already supplies.
items.provenance: Authored for CIE 9702 AS Physics topic 2 from the topic claim ledger and work order.
objective_titles: determine displacement from the area under a velocity–time graph

items.prompt: A tractor's displacement–time graph is a straight line from (0, 0) to (25 s, 150 m). Determine its velocity, with the reasoning.
items.canonical_answer: On a displacement–time graph the gradient gives the velocity. The line is straight, so v = ∆s ÷ ∆t = 150 ÷ 25 = 6.0 m s⁻¹, and because the line is straight this value holds along the whole stretch: the tractor moves at 6.0 m s⁻¹ throughout.
marking_guidance: Reading the graph: the gradient of the straight line taken as ∆s ÷ ∆t - 1 mark.
What the gradient means: the velocity, 150 ÷ 25 = 6.0 m s⁻¹, constant along the line - 1 mark.
items.provenance: Authored for CIE 9702 AS Physics topic 2 from the topic claim ledger and work order.
objective_titles: determine velocity using the gradient of a displacement–time graph

items.prompt: A ball rolls up a slope. Its displacement–time graph is a straight line rising from (0, 0) to a highest point at (4.0 s, 12 m), then a straight line falling to (10 s, 0). Determine its velocity on the way up and on the way down.
items.canonical_answer: Way up: the gradient of the rising line, 12 ÷ 4.0 = 3.0 m s⁻¹ up the slope. Way down: the falling line runs from (4.0, 12) to (10, 0), so ∆s = 0 − 12 = −12 m over ∆t = 6.0 s, giving −2.0 m s⁻¹; the negative sign means motion back down the slope, towards the starting point.
marking_guidance: Reading the graph: the two gradients taken separately, 12 ÷ 4.0 and −12 ÷ 6.0 - 1 mark.
What the values mean: the graph shows 3.0 m s⁻¹ up and −2.0 m s⁻¹, so the value gives the return direction down the slope - 1 mark.
items.provenance: Authored for CIE 9702 AS Physics topic 2 from the topic claim ledger and work order.
objective_titles: determine velocity using the gradient of a displacement–time graph

items.prompt: A delivery van's displacement–time graph is a straight line passing through (20 s, 280 m) and (80 s, 910 m). Determine its velocity from the gradient of the line.
items.canonical_answer: On a displacement–time graph v = ∆s ÷ ∆t. Here ∆s = 910 − 280 = 630 m and ∆t = 80 − 20 = 60 s, so v = 630 ÷ 60 = 10.5 m s⁻¹, which is 11 m s⁻¹ to two significant figures.
marking_guidance: Equation and substitution: v = ∆s ÷ ∆t with 630 m over 60 s - 1 mark.
Final answer: 10.5 m s⁻¹, given as 11 m s⁻¹ to two significant figures, with the unit - 1 mark.
items.provenance: Authored for CIE 9702 AS Physics topic 2 from the topic claim ledger and work order.
objective_titles: determine velocity using the gradient of a displacement–time graph

items.prompt: A cyclist's displacement–time graph is a curve that gets less steep as time goes on, without any straight stretch. Explain how her velocity is found at 20 s, and why the answer cannot come from one difference across the whole graph.
items.canonical_answer: At 20 s the velocity is the gradient of the tangent drawn to the curve at that point. Across a curved stretch there is no single velocity: the gradient changes from moment to moment, so one difference of endpoints gives only the average velocity over the interval. In this situation the curve flattens, so the tangent's gradient - and her velocity - is smaller at 20 s than at the start.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the reason - here the curve means a changing gradient, so the velocity at one instant needs the tangent at 20 s, whereas the endpoints give only the average because the slope changes between them.
items.provenance: Authored for CIE 9702 AS Physics topic 2 from the topic claim ledger and work order.
objective_titles: determine velocity using the gradient of a displacement–time graph

items.prompt: State the features of a displacement–time graph on which a body at rest and a body moving with constant velocity can be told apart.
items.canonical_answer: A body at rest gives a horizontal line: zero gradient, so zero velocity. A body with constant velocity gives a straight sloping line: one gradient, so one velocity along the whole stretch. A curve means a velocity that is changing. The feature that separates rest from steady motion is the slope of the line.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the features - horizontal for rest, straight and sloping for constant velocity, with the gradient as the quantity that differs.
items.provenance: Authored for CIE 9702 AS Physics topic 2 from the topic claim ledger and work order.
objective_titles: determine velocity using the gradient of a displacement–time graph

items.prompt: State the difference between the gradient of a chord drawn across a curved displacement–time graph and the gradient of a tangent drawn at one point of it.
items.canonical_answer: The chord joins two points of the curve, and its gradient is the average velocity over that interval. The tangent touches the curve at one instant, and its gradient is the velocity at that instant. They differ because the curve's gradient changes; on a straight stretch the two would agree.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the contrast - the chord gives the average velocity over an interval whereas the tangent gives the velocity at one instant; both are gradients but of different lines.
items.provenance: Authored for CIE 9702 AS Physics topic 2 from the topic claim ledger and work order.
objective_titles: determine velocity using the gradient of a displacement–time graph

items.prompt: Explain why a steeper straight line on a displacement–time graph means a faster body.
items.canonical_answer: The gradient of a displacement–time graph is the velocity. A steeper line rises by more displacement in the same width of time, so ∆s ÷ ∆t is larger, and the velocity the gradient gives is larger. The body covers ground faster, which is what the graph's slope is needed to show.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the reason - the gradient is the velocity, so more rise in the same time means a larger ∆s ÷ ∆t, and the purpose of the slope is exactly to display this.
items.provenance: Authored for CIE 9702 AS Physics topic 2 from the topic claim ledger and work order.
objective_titles: determine velocity using the gradient of a displacement–time graph

items.prompt: A car's velocity–time graph is a straight line from (0, 5.0 m s⁻¹) to (12 s, 20 m s⁻¹). Determine its acceleration, with the reasoning.
items.canonical_answer: On a velocity–time graph the gradient gives the acceleration. Here a = ∆v ÷ ∆t = (20 − 5.0) ÷ 12 = 15 ÷ 12 = 1.25 m s⁻², which is 1.3 m s⁻² to two significant figures, directed along the motion.
marking_guidance: Reading the graph: the gradient taken as ∆v ÷ ∆t with the change of 15 m s⁻¹ over 12 s - 1 mark.
What the gradient means: the acceleration, 15 ÷ 12 = 1.25 m s⁻², given as 1.3 m s⁻² to two significant figures - 1 mark.
items.provenance: Authored for CIE 9702 AS Physics topic 2 from the topic claim ledger and work order.
objective_titles: determine acceleration using the gradient of a velocity–time graph

items.prompt: A cart rolls up a ramp and back down. Its velocity–time graph is a straight line from (0, 6.0 m s⁻¹) to (4.0 s, −6.0 m s⁻¹), taking up the slope as positive. Determine its acceleration over the 4.0 s and why that value is the same on the way up as on the way down.
items.canonical_answer: The acceleration is the gradient: a = ∆v ÷ ∆t = (−6.0 − 6.0) ÷ 4.0 = −12 ÷ 4.0 = −3.0 m s⁻², so 3.0 m s⁻² down the slope. Because the line is straight, one gradient covers the whole flight: the velocity falls steadily from 6.0 m s⁻¹ through zero to −6.0 m s⁻¹, so the acceleration is −3.0 m s⁻² both while the cart slows going up and while it speeds up coming down.
marking_guidance: Reading the graph: the gradient as −12 ÷ 4.0 - 1 mark.
What the value gives: the acceleration −3.0 m s⁻², the same up and down because the line is straight, so one gradient holds throughout - 1 mark.
items.provenance: Authored for CIE 9702 AS Physics topic 2 from the topic claim ledger and work order.
objective_titles: determine acceleration using the gradient of a velocity–time graph

items.prompt: A tuk-tuk's velocity–time graph is a straight line through (4.0 s, 3.0 m s⁻¹) and (16 s, 7.5 m s⁻¹). Determine its acceleration from the gradient.
items.canonical_answer: a = ∆v ÷ ∆t. Here ∆v = 7.5 − 3.0 = 4.5 m s⁻¹ and ∆t = 16 − 4.0 = 12 s, so a = 4.5 ÷ 12 = 0.375 m s⁻², which is 0.38 m s⁻² to two significant figures.
marking_guidance: Equation and substitution: a = ∆v ÷ ∆t with 4.5 m s⁻¹ over 12 s - 1 mark.
Final answer: 0.375 m s⁻², given as 0.38 m s⁻² to two significant figures, with the unit - 1 mark.
items.provenance: Authored for CIE 9702 AS Physics topic 2 from the topic claim ledger and work order.
objective_titles: determine acceleration using the gradient of a velocity–time graph

items.prompt: On a velocity–time graph, one stretch of a motorbike's line is horizontal at 25 m s⁻¹ and the next stretch falls as a straight line. Explain why the motorbike is accelerating in the second stretch but not the first, and whether the falling line means it is reversing.
items.canonical_answer: The acceleration is the gradient of the line. In the first stretch the gradient is zero, so the velocity holds at 25 m s⁻¹. In the second the gradient is negative, so there is an acceleration directed against the motion and the motorbike is slowing. It is not reversing: the line is still above the axis, so the velocity is still positive, and only if the line crossed the axis would the motion reverse.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the reasoning for this case - acceleration follows the gradient, so a horizontal line is zero and a falling straight line is a negative acceleration, meaning slowing here because the line stays above the axis.
items.provenance: Authored for CIE 9702 AS Physics topic 2 from the topic claim ledger and work order.
objective_titles: determine acceleration using the gradient of a velocity–time graph

items.prompt: A learner reads the acceleration of a car from a velocity–time graph by looking up the height of the line at 6.0 s and reporting "10 m s⁻²". Explain the error and how the acceleration is actually found.
items.canonical_answer: The height of the line is the velocity, not the acceleration: at 6.0 s the car is moving at 10 m s⁻¹, and the unit of the reading shows it. The acceleration is the gradient of the line: the change in the height divided by the time over which it changes. The test is whether the question is about the slope of the line or its height; a slope question is answered with ∆v ÷ ∆t, never with a single reading.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the error named - a reading of the height confused with the gradient; the height is the velocity, and the acceleration needs ∆v ÷ ∆t instead.
items.provenance: Authored for CIE 9702 AS Physics topic 2 from the topic claim ledger and work order.
objective_titles: determine acceleration using the gradient of a velocity–time graph

items.prompt: State the three quantities a velocity–time graph carries, and where each is found on it.
items.canonical_answer: The height of the line gives the velocity at that time; the gradient of the line gives the acceleration; the area between the line and the time axis gives the displacement.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the three features - height for velocity, gradient for acceleration, area for displacement, each tied to where it is read.

items.prompt: State the difference between what the height of a velocity–time graph shows and what its gradient shows.
items.canonical_answer: The height shows the velocity at that instant, read straight off the axis. The gradient shows the acceleration, the rate at which the velocity is changing. A line can be high and flat - fast, not accelerating - or low and steep - slow, but gathering speed quickly.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the contrast - the height is the velocity whereas the gradient is the acceleration, so both can be read from one line and they answer different questions.

objective_titles: determine acceleration using the gradient of a velocity–time graph

items.prompt: When a gradient of a velocity–time graph is used to find an acceleration, explain why the two points are taken far apart on the line rather than close together.
items.canonical_answer: Each reading of a graph carries a small uncertainty. The gradient is a difference, so the same reading uncertainty is divided by a larger ∆v and ∆t when the points are far apart, making the fraction of error in ∆v ÷ ∆t smaller. The purpose of choosing widely separated points is to make the uncertainty of the answer small compared with the answer itself.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the reason - the reading uncertainty is fixed, so a larger difference across the points makes the percentage uncertainty of the gradient smaller, which is why a wide span is needed.
items.provenance: Authored for CIE 9702 AS Physics topic 2 from the topic claim ledger and work order.
objective_titles: determine acceleration using the gradient of a velocity–time graph

items.prompt: Show, from the definitions of velocity and acceleration, that a body with uniform acceleration travels a distance s = ut + ½at² in time t.
items.canonical_answer: Start with the definition of acceleration, a = (v − u) ÷ t, which for uniform acceleration gives the velocity–time graph as a straight line from u to v over a width t. The displacement is the area under that line. Take the area as a rectangle of height u and width t, which is ut, plus a triangle of height (v − u) = at and width t, which is ½at². So the total area, and so the distance, is s = ut + ½at². The steps run in order from the definition to the graph to the area, and the result is the equation stated.
marking_guidance: Order of steps: first the definition a = (v − u) ÷ t, then the straight-line graph it gives, then the area split into rectangle and triangle - 1 mark for the sequence started from the definitions.
The result: the areas ut and ½at² added, so the derivation gives s = ut + ½at² as required - 1 mark.
items.provenance: Authored for CIE 9702 AS Physics topic 2 from the topic claim ledger and work order.
objective_titles: derive, from the definitions of velocity and acceleration, equations that represent uniformly accelerated motion in a straight line

items.prompt: A mango stone is flicked along the ground at 1.8 m s⁻¹ and stops after 0.90 m. Show that its acceleration was about −1.8 m s⁻².
items.canonical_answer: Use v² = u² + 2as, because the time is neither given nor wanted. Substitution: 0 = 1.8² + 2 × a × 0.90, so 2 × 0.90 × a = −3.24, which gives a = −3.24 ÷ 1.80 = −1.80 m s⁻². The answer to three significant figures, −1.80 m s⁻², is the value the question rounds to −1.8 m s⁻².
marking_guidance: Equation and substitution: v² = u² + 2as with 0 = 1.8² + 2 × a × 0.90 - 1 mark.
Final answer: a = −3.24 ÷ 1.80 = −1.80 m s⁻², which shows the stated value, with the unit - 1 mark.

items.prompt: A problem gives u, v and a, and asks for the distance travelled. Explain why v² = u² + 2as is the equation to use, and what would be lost by reaching first for s = ut + ½at².
items.canonical_answer: The situation supplies u, v and a and wants s: the time is neither given nor asked. v² = u² + 2as links exactly those four and passes the time by, so the answer comes in one substitution. In this case s = ut + ½at² holds the missing t, so using it means stopping to find the time first from v = u + at - an extra step in which a slip is easy - before the distance can be reached at all.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the reason - the equation is picked by which quantity is absent; here the time is missing, so the form without t is needed, because the ones carrying t cannot be used without stopping to find it first.
items.provenance: Authored for CIE 9702 AS Physics topic 2 from the topic claim ledger and work order.

items.prompt: State the feature that all the equations of uniformly accelerated motion share, and the condition under which each of them holds.
items.canonical_answer: Each equation links four of the five quantities s, u, v, a and t, and leaves one out; each holds for uniform acceleration in a straight line. An equation is chosen by the quantity it leaves out: the one whose missing quantity is neither given nor wanted fits the problem.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the features - four of the five quantities linked, uniform straight-line acceleration as the condition, and selection by the absent quantity.

items.prompt: State the difference between s = ut + ½at² and s = ½(u + v)t as ways of finding the same displacement.
items.canonical_answer: Both hold for uniform acceleration, and both are the area under the same velocity–time line. s = ut + ½at² takes the area as a rectangle plus a triangle, so it needs u, a and t. s = ½(u + v)t takes it as a trapezium - the average velocity times the time - so it needs u, v and t and never mentions a. The difference is which quantities each form uses, and so which problem each fits.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the contrast - the same area split differently: one form uses u, a, t whereas the other uses the average velocity ½(u + v) with u, v, t, so unlike the first it leaves the acceleration out.
items.provenance: Authored for CIE 9702 AS Physics topic 2 from the topic claim ledger and work order.
objective_titles: derive, from the definitions of velocity and acceleration, equations that represent uniformly accelerated motion in a straight line

items.prompt: The equation s = ½(u + v)t contains the average of the start and end velocities. Explain why the plain average of u and v is the correct average velocity here, and when it would not be.
items.canonical_answer: On a velocity–time graph the area is the displacement, and the average velocity is the displacement divided by the time, so the average is the mean height of the line. For uniform acceleration the line is straight, so its mean height is halfway between its ends, ½(u + v). If the acceleration were not uniform, the line would curve, and the mean height would no longer sit halfway between the end values; the average velocity would then have to come from the whole area, and ½(u + v) would misstate it.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the reason - a straight line has a mean height halfway between u and v, so the purpose of ½(u + v) is exact only under uniform acceleration, and a curve would need the area taken instead.

items.prompt: State the equation of motion that describes free fall, with the value and direction of the acceleration it uses.
items.canonical_answer: Free fall is uniformly accelerated motion with a = g = 9.81 m s⁻² directed downward throughout the fall, whatever the mass: s = ut + ½gt², with u = 0 for a body released from rest.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the equation with g = 9.81 m s⁻² downward named; the definition of free fall as uniform acceleration independent of mass carries the mark.

items.prompt: A hammer slides off a flat roof 6.0 m above the ground, starting from rest. Calculate the speed at which it strikes the ground.
items.canonical_answer: v² = u² + 2as, with u = 0 and a = g = 9.81 m s⁻². Substitution: v² = 2 × 9.81 × 6.0, so v² = 117.7, and v is the square root of 117.7 = 10.8 m s⁻¹, which is 11 m s⁻¹ to two significant figures.
marking_guidance: Equation and substitution: v² = u² + 2as with 2 × 9.81 × 6.0 = 117.7 - 1 mark.
Final answer: 10.8 m s⁻¹, given as 11 m s⁻¹ to two significant figures, with the unit - 1 mark.

items.prompt: A ball is thrown straight up at 12 m s⁻¹ from a point 1.5 m above the ground. Taking up as positive, calculate the time it takes to reach its highest point.
items.canonical_answer: At the highest point the velocity is zero. With up positive, a = −9.81 m s⁻². v = u + at, so 0 = 12 + (−9.81) × t, which gives t = 12 ÷ 9.81 = 1.22 s, which is 1.2 s to two significant figures.
marking_guidance: Equation and substitution: v = u + at with 0 = 12 − 9.81t, the signs kept consistent with up positive - 1 mark.
Final answer: 12 ÷ 9.81 = 1.22 s, given as 1.2 s to two significant figures, with the unit - 1 mark.

items.prompt: A brick is thrown straight down from a bridge 35 m above a river, at 4.0 m s⁻¹. Taking down as positive, calculate the time before it hits the water.
items.canonical_answer: s = ut + ½at², with down positive: 35 = 4.0t + ½ × 9.81 × t². So 4.905t² + 4.0t − 35 = 0. The quadratic gives t = (−4.0 + the square root of (16.0 + 4 × 4.905 × 35)) ÷ (2 × 4.905) = (−4.0 + 26.3) ÷ 9.81 = 22.3 ÷ 9.81 = 2.27 s, which is 2.3 s to two significant figures.
marking_guidance: Equation and substitution: s = ut + ½at² set up as 35 = 4.0t + 4.905t² with down positive - 1 mark.
Final answer: t = 22.3 ÷ 9.81 = 2.27 s, given as 2.3 s to two significant figures, with the unit - 1 mark.
items.provenance: Authored for CIE 9702 AS Physics topic 2 from the topic claim ledger and work order.

items.prompt: A problem says a car passes a speed camera at 15 m s⁻¹ and brakes to a halt. A learner puts u = 0 in the first equation she writes. Explain the error and how u is found.
items.canonical_answer: The error is assuming the car started from rest because the question did not say so. In this situation the car is moving when the problem opens, so u = 15 m s⁻¹; it is the finishing velocity that is zero, because the car brakes to a halt. The initial and final velocities are read from the situation: the question must actually state rest, at the start or the end, before a zero can be written for u or v. Here only v is zero.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the error named - a zero written for a velocity the question never states; in fact the passage of the camera gives u = 15 m s⁻¹ and only the halt gives v = 0, so the values must be read from the situation instead of assumed.

items.prompt: A learner takes up as positive for a ball thrown upward, then uses a = +9.81 m s⁻² "because the ball is moving up at the start". Explain the error and give the sign the acceleration actually carries.
items.canonical_answer: The acceleration's sign does not follow the motion's direction; it follows the positive direction chosen. Up is positive, and gravity acts downward throughout the flight, so a = −9.81 m s⁻² while the ball rises, at the top, and while it falls. The error is inconsistent signs: one direction chosen, then abandoned for the acceleration. With up positive, s, u, v and a all take their signs from that single choice.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the error named - the sign of a switched to match the motion instead of the chosen positive direction; in fact a = −9.81 m s⁻² throughout with up positive, because every vector takes its sign from that one choice.

items.prompt: A scooter accelerates uniformly from rest to 18 m s⁻¹ over 60 m. A learner divides 60 by the 6.7 s the run took and calls the answer the final velocity. Explain the error and give the value the division actually produces.
items.canonical_answer: Distance divided by time gives the average speed, not a velocity at the end. For this motion, with uniform acceleration, the average velocity is ½(u + v) = ½ × 18 = 9.0 m s⁻¹ - and that is the 9.0 the division produces. The final velocity of 18 m s⁻¹ must come from the uniformly accelerated equations, such as v² = u² + 2as. The test is whether the velocity is changing; when it is, distance ÷ time cannot give a final value.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the error named - an average mistaken for a final value; in fact distance ÷ time gives the average speed, here 9.0 m s⁻¹, and the final velocity instead needs the equations of uniformly accelerated motion.

items.prompt: State two features of the motion of a body falling freely that the equations of uniformly accelerated motion rely on.

items.prompt: State the difference between the velocity and the acceleration of a ball at the top of its vertical flight.
items.canonical_answer: At the top the velocity is zero for an instant: the ball has stopped rising and not yet fallen. The acceleration is 9.81 m s⁻² downward, unchanged from the rest of the flight. The difference is that velocity is what is changing, and acceleration is the rate at which it changes; zero velocity coexists with a nonzero acceleration because gravity has not stopped acting.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the contrast - the velocity is zero at the top whereas the acceleration stays 9.81 m s⁻² downward, and the two are different quantities, one being the rate of change of the other.

items.prompt: Describe an experiment to determine the acceleration of free fall using a falling object. Include what is measured, with which instruments, and how g follows from the readings.
items.canonical_answer: First, the apparatus: a dense steel ball is held in an electromagnet or release clamp above a trapdoor or light gate, both connected to an electronic timer - the release starts the clock and the arrival at the bottom stops it. Then the measurements: the height of fall h is measured with a metre rule held vertical, from the ball's release point to the detector, and the fall time t is read from the timer. Readings are repeated at each height and averaged, to reduce the effect of random error, and the height is varied over at least six values so a graph can be drawn. The result follows two ways: for one fall, h = ½gt², so g = 2h ÷ t²; better, h is plotted against t², giving a straight line through the origin whose gradient is g ÷ 2, so g is twice the gradient, in m s⁻².
marking_guidance: Order of the steps: first the release-and-time apparatus, then the height with a metre rule and the time with the timer, then the repeats and the varied heights - 1 mark for the sequence and the instruments named.
What is measured and how: the height h and the fall time t, with repeats averaged - 1 mark.
The result: g = 2h ÷ t², or the graph of h against t² whose gradient gives g when doubled - 1 mark, so the readings give the final value.
items.provenance: Authored for CIE 9702 AS Physics topic 2 from the topic claim ledger and work order.
objective_titles: describe an experiment to determine the acceleration of free fall using a falling object

items.prompt: In a free-fall experiment a hand-held stopwatch is used to time a ball falling 0.80 m, and the timing is repeated and averaged. Describe two limitations of this method and the effect each has on the value of g found.
items.canonical_answer: One limitation is the human reaction time, about 0.2 s, added to every reading of a fall that lasts under 0.41 s; the measured time is larger than the true one, and because g = 2h ÷ t², an over-large t makes g come out too small. A second limitation is that repeating and averaging reduces only random scatter: the reaction time is a systematic error that shifts every reading the same way, so the repeats leave the value of g biased low and only a taller drop - which makes the fixed delay a smaller fraction of the measured time - or electronic timing reduces the effect.
marking_guidance: Limitations and their effect: the reaction time of about 0.2 s inflates t, which lowers g because g = 2h ÷ t² - 1 mark.
Because repeating reduces only random error, the systematic delay survives the averaging, so the repeats cannot rescue the value - 1 mark.
items.provenance: Authored for CIE 9702 AS Physics topic 2 from the topic claim ledger and work order.
objective_titles: describe an experiment to determine the acceleration of free fall using a falling object

items.prompt: A class's free-fall timings are taken with a hand stopwatch, and their value of g comes out as 7.2 m s⁻². Another class, using an electronic trapdoor timer over the same heights, gets 9.6 m s⁻². Explain the difference between the two results.
items.canonical_answer: Both differences trace to the timing. A hand stopwatch adds a reaction delay of about 0.2 s to each fall, which makes the measured t too large and, since g = 2h ÷ t², pulls g down towards the 7.2 m s⁻² the first class found. The electronic timer removes that human delay, so the second class's t is closer to the true fall time and their g, 9.6 m s⁻², sits nearer to 9.81 m s⁻². In this situation the pattern of the two values - the coarser timing giving the lower g - is exactly what an inflated t produces.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the reasoning - the hand timing carries a systematic human delay that inflates t and so lowers g through g = 2h ÷ t², whereas the electronic readings, free of that delay, give a value closer to 9.81 m s⁻²; the case is explained by the timing alone.
items.provenance: Authored for CIE 9702 AS Physics topic 2 from the topic claim ledger and work order.
objective_titles: describe an experiment to determine the acceleration of free fall using a falling object

items.prompt: State the two features of a graph of fall height against time squared that make it useful for finding g.
items.canonical_answer: The points lie on a straight line through the origin, and its gradient is g ÷ 2, so doubling the gradient gives g in m s⁻². A straight line through six points also exposes any single reading that is out of line, which one pair of readings cannot.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the features - a straight line through the origin, with gradient g ÷ 2 so that g is twice it, in m s⁻².

items.prompt: State the difference between timing a free fall electronically and timing it with a hand-held stopwatch, for finding g.
items.canonical_answer: Electronic timing measures the fall alone: the clock starts at the release and stops at the arrival, so the measured t is close to the true fall time. A hand stopwatch measures the fall plus a human reaction delay of about 0.2 s, so t is systematically too large, and since g = 2h ÷ t², the value of g comes out systematically too small. The difference between the methods is which errors they carry: a small random scatter in the electronic method, against a large systematic bias in the hand-held one.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the contrast - electronic timing gives t close to the true value whereas hand timing adds a systematic reaction delay that inflates t and so lowers g; the difference is stated as the error each method carries.

items.prompt: In the free-fall experiment, explain why the fall time is measured at several different heights rather than once at one height.
items.canonical_answer: Several heights are needed because the result is taken from a graph of h against t²: a line needs more than one point, and only a line through a spread of points gives a reliable gradient, which is where g comes from. With one height there is one pair of readings and no check on it. A spread of heights also shows up a bad reading as a point off the line, which a single measurement cannot reveal, and a larger height makes the fixed timing uncertainty a smaller fraction of the measured time.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the reason - the gradient method needs a line drawn through several points, so several heights are needed; the repeats and the spread together expose scatter and out-of-line readings, which one pair of readings cannot.

items.prompt: State the equation that governs the perpendicular axis of a body whose velocity is uniform in one direction while a uniform acceleration acts at right angles to it, and the shape of the path that follows.
items.canonical_answer: Along the accelerated axis the uniformly accelerated equations hold, s = ut + ½at² with the initial velocity along that axis; along the axis of constant velocity the distance is simply velocity × time. The path is a parabola.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the equation for the accelerated axis, with the constant-velocity axis named as distance = velocity × time, and the parabolic path stated; the definition of the motion is the two separate rules.
items.provenance: Authored for CIE 9702 AS Physics topic 2 from the topic claim ledger and work order.

items.prompt: State the path feature that results when a uniform velocity in one direction is combined with a uniform acceleration at right angles to it, and the quantity that is shared between the two directions.
items.canonical_answer: The path is a parabola. The two directions are treated separately - the velocity component along the first axis stays constant while the perpendicular component changes at a constant rate - and the time is the one quantity shared between them.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the parabolic path and the shared time named as the feature that joins the two separate descriptions.

items.prompt: A ball is kicked at 15 m s⁻¹ at 40° above the horizontal. A learner uses the full 15 m s⁻¹ in v = u + at to find the time to the highest point, and later adds the horizontal and vertical velocities as plain numbers. Explain both errors and give the correct treatment.
items.canonical_answer: Both errors come from ignoring components. Gravity acts vertically only, so the vertical motion uses the component 15 sin 40° = 9.64 m s⁻¹, not the whole 15 m s⁻¹; the horizontal component 15 cos 40° = 11.5 m s⁻¹ is untouched by gravity and forms no part of a vertical equation. And because the two components are perpendicular, they cannot be added as numbers: the speed at any point combines them by Pythagoras, the square root of the sum of their squares. The correct treatment is two separate motions sharing one time: vertical component with g, horizontal component unchanged.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the errors named - the whole velocity used in the vertical equation, and perpendicular components added as numbers; the correct idea is the split into 15 sin 40° vertical and 15 cos 40° horizontal, combined by Pythagoras instead.
items.provenance: Authored for CIE 9702 AS Physics topic 2 from the topic claim ledger and work order.
objective_titles: describe and explain motion due to a uniform velocity in one direction and a uniform acceleration in a perpendicular direction

items.prompt: State the difference between the velocity component of a projectile along the horizontal axis and the one along the vertical axis, during the flight.
items.canonical_answer: The horizontal component stays constant throughout the flight, because no acceleration acts along it. The vertical component changes at a constant 9.81 m s⁻¹ each second, decreasing on the way up, passing through zero, and growing downward on the way down. Both components exist at every point of the path; they differ in whether gravity reaches them.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the contrast - the horizontal component is constant whereas the vertical component changes uniformly under g, because the acceleration acts on the vertical axis alone.

items.prompt:
Twelve questions. Choose one option for each.

1. Which quantity is a vector?
A  distance
B  speed
C  displacement
D  time

2. A car travels 8.0 km north, then 3.0 km south, in 20 min. What is the magnitude of its displacement?
A  11 km
B  8.0 km
C  5.0 km
D  3.0 km

3. On a displacement–time graph, what does the gradient of the line give?
A  acceleration
B  velocity
C  displacement
D  distance

4. On a velocity–time graph, what does the area between the line and the time axis give?
A  acceleration
B  velocity
C  displacement
D  gradient

5. A velocity–time graph is a straight line from (0, 0) to (4.0 s, 12 m s⁻¹). What is the acceleration?
A  3.0 m s⁻²
B  12 m s⁻²
C  48 m s⁻²
D  zero

6. A body accelerates uniformly from rest at 2.0 m s⁻² for 5.0 s. What distance does it cover?
A  10 m
B  25 m
C  50 m
D  5.0 m

7. A stone is dropped from rest and falls for 2.0 s. Taking g = 9.81 m s⁻², what is its speed after 2.0 s?
A  4.91 m s⁻¹
B  9.81 m s⁻¹
C  19.6 m s⁻¹
D  39.2 m s⁻¹

8. At the highest point of a ball's vertical flight, what is its acceleration, taking up as positive?
A  zero
B  −9.81 m s⁻²
C  +9.81 m s⁻²
D  −9.81 m s⁻¹

9. A train accelerates uniformly from 3.0 m s⁻¹ to 9.0 m s⁻¹ in 12 s. What is its displacement in that time?
A  72 m
B  108 m
C  36 m
D  54 m

10. Which pair of quantities has the same unit?
A  distance and speed
B  speed and acceleration
C  velocity and acceleration
D  speed and velocity

11. A projectile is moving with horizontal velocity component 4.0 m s⁻¹ and vertical component 3.0 m s⁻¹. What is its speed?
A  7.0 m s⁻¹
B  1.0 m s⁻¹
C  5.0 m s⁻¹
D  12 m s⁻¹

12. A ball rolls off a table 0.45 m high at 1.2 m s⁻¹. Taking g = 9.81 m s⁻², roughly how far from the table's foot does it land?
A  1.1 m
B  0.36 m
C  0.23 m
D  0.55 m
items.canonical_answer:
Key: 1 C, 2 C, 3 B, 4 C, 5 A, 6 B, 7 C, 8 B, 9 A, 10 D, 11 C, 12 B.
1. C: displacement has magnitude and direction. A and B are the scalar partners, the error of treating a vector as its scalar twin; D is a scalar that never has a direction.
2. C: 8.0 − 3.0 = 5.0 km. A adds the distances, the error of using the scalar path total where the vector change is asked; B ignores the return leg; D reports the return leg alone.
3. B: the gradient of a displacement–time graph is the velocity. A is the confusion of this graph with a velocity–time graph; C and D are the axis quantity and its scalar partner, read as if the question were about height.
4. C: the area under a velocity–time line is the displacement. A confuses the area with the gradient; B is the height of the line, the error of reading a value where a region is asked; D names the property that gives the acceleration instead.
5. A: the gradient is 12 ÷ 4.0 = 3.0 m s⁻². B reads the height of the line instead of its slope; C multiplies the two axis values; D treats the straight sloping line as if it were horizontal.
6. B: s = ½at², so with a = 2.0 m s⁻² and t = 5.0 s the distance is 25 m. A uses v = at as a distance; C doubles instead of halving; D uses s = ut with the final velocity mistaken as u.
7. C: v = gt = 9.81 × 2.0 = 19.6 m s⁻¹. A halves the product instead of the time; B reports g itself as a speed; D squares the time inside a linear equation.
8. B: gravity still acts, so a = −9.81 m s⁻². A is the error that zero velocity means zero acceleration; C flips the sign against the chosen positive direction; D carries the unit of velocity, not acceleration.
9. A: s = ½(u + v)t = ½ × 12 × 12 = 72 m. B uses the final velocity alone, dropping the average to its top value; C uses the initial alone; D uses s = ut + ½at² with a = 0.5 m s⁻² but halves the wrong term.
10. D: both are in m s⁻¹. A pairs a length with a speed; B and C pair a speed with an acceleration, the commonest unit slip.
11. C: the components are perpendicular, so the speed is the square root of (16 + 9) = 5.0 m s⁻¹. A adds them as numbers, the vector error; B subtracts them; D multiplies them.
12. B: the fall takes t = the square root of (2 × 0.45 ÷ 9.81) = 0.303 s, and 1.2 × 0.303 = 0.36 m. A uses the height as the fall time; C uses ½g instead of g in the fall; D divides the height by the horizontal velocity, mixing the axes.
marking_guidance: The key: one mark per correct option, twelve marks in all.

Every distractor is a named error: a scalar swapped for its vector partner, a height read where a gradient is asked, an area taken as a triangle from a non-zero start, a sign flipped, components added as plain numbers.

items.prompt:
A lift in an office block in Windhoek starts at rest and accelerates uniformly upward at 1.5 m s⁻² for 3.0 s.
(a) Define acceleration. [1]
(b) Determine the velocity of the lift after 3.0 s. [2]
(c) Determine the distance travelled in the 3.0 s. [2]
(d) The lift then decelerates uniformly to rest in 2.0 s. Determine the deceleration. [1]
(e) Explain why the lift's acceleration is the same value at every instant while it decelerates, even though its velocity is falling. [2]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, a = (v − u) ÷ t, with unit m s⁻².
(b) v = u + at, so v = 0 + (1.5 × 3.0) = 4.5 m s⁻¹ upward.
(c) s = ut + ½at² = 0 + ½ × (1.5 × 9.0) = 6.75 m, which is 6.8 m to two significant figures.
(d) a = ∆v ÷ ∆t = (0 − 4.5) ÷ 2.0 = −2.25 m s⁻², so the deceleration is 2.3 m s⁻² to two significant figures.
(e) Because the change of velocity is uniform, ∆v ÷ ∆t is the same for every interval chosen: the velocity falls by the same amount each second. The acceleration is the rate of change, so with a uniform change the rate is constant, at −2.25 m s⁻², while the velocity itself passes through different values.
marking_guidance: Part (a): 1 mark for the definition with rate of change of velocity and its unit named.
Parts (b) and (c): 2 marks each - the equation v = u + at and s = ut + ½at² with correct substitutions, 1 mark for the working and 1 mark for each answer with its unit.
Part (d): 1 mark for a = ∆v ÷ ∆t with the answer 2.25 m s⁻² and its unit.

Part (e): 2 marks - because the rate of change of velocity is uniform, the gradient is one constant value, and the reason is that a falling velocity with an unchanging rate still gives a constant acceleration.

items.prompt: A watermelon rolls off the flat bed of a bakkie parked outside a cuca shop. The bed is 1.25 m above the road and the watermelon leaves the edge moving horizontally at 0.80 m s⁻¹. Air resistance is negligible. (a) Calculate the time the watermelon takes to fall. (b) Calculate the horizontal distance from the edge of the bed to where it lands. (c) Calculate the speed at which it strikes the road.
items.canonical_answer:
(a) The vertical fall sets the time: h = ½gt², so t² = 2h ÷ g = (2 × 1.25) ÷ 9.81 = 2.50 ÷ 9.81 = 0.2548, so t = 0.505 s, which is 0.51 s to two significant figures.
(b) Horizontally the velocity is constant: x = 0.80 × 0.505 = 0.404 m, which is 0.40 m to two significant figures.
(c) The vertical component on landing is vy = g × t = 9.81 × 0.505 = 4.95 m s⁻¹; the horizontal component stays 0.80 m s⁻¹. The speed is the square root of (0.80² + 4.95²) = the square root of (0.64 + 24.5) = the square root of 25.14 = 5.01 m s⁻¹, which is 5.0 m s⁻¹ to two significant figures. Each answer is rounded once, at the end, and given to two significant figures, the precision of the data.
marking_guidance: Equation: h = ½gt² for the fall, with the two axes treated separately - 1 mark.
Substitution and working: t² = 2.50 ÷ 9.81 = 0.2548 so t = 0.505 s, then x = 0.80 × 0.505 = 0.404 m - 1 mark.
The components on landing: vy = 9.81 × 0.505 = 4.95 m s⁻¹ alongside the constant 0.80 m s⁻¹ - 1 mark.
The speed combined by Pythagoras, the square root of 25.14 = 5.01 m s⁻¹ - 1 mark.
Answer: 5.0 m s⁻¹ with its unit, stated to two significant figures and justified by the precision of the data - 1 mark.
